GMC guidance: doctors cannot be compelled to participate in assisted dying even if it were legal; must provide good end-of-life care; must explore patient suffering compassionately; may discuss legal alternatives (advance decisions, palliative sedation, hospice care). Helping a patient travel abroad for assisted dying (where legal, e.g., Switzerland — Dignitas) is a complex legal area — GPs should take legal advice. Palliative sedation (appropriately titrated sedation to relieve suffering) is legal and distinct from assisted dying.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Assisted dying is illegal in the UK as of 2024 (legislation may change — check current law).
explanation.B: CORRECT — Assisted dying illegal in UK. GP must not assist. Must compassionately explore suffering, provide palliative care and legal alternatives. Document.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Assisting a patient to access assisted dying services (including travel to Switzerland) is a complex legal grey area — GPs should seek legal advice before providing such assistance.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Expressing a wish to die in the context of severe depression requires compassionate exploration and mental health support — not social services referral.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Palliative sedation (appropriately titrated symptom relief) is legal and entirely distinct from assisted dying — this is a critical distinction.

reference: Suicide Act 1961. GMC — End of life care. Terminally Ill Adults (End of Life) Bill 2024. https://www.gmc-uk.org/ethical-guidance/ethical-guidance-for-doctors/treatment-and-care-towards-the-end-of-life

question: A GP receives a complaint from a patient who feels their concerns were not listened to during a consultation. Per the NHS Complaints Procedure (NHS England Complaints Regulations 2009, updated 2023), how should the practice respond?

options.A: Ignore complaints — patients have no formal right to complain about GPs
options.B: Acknowledge the complaint within 3 working days; attempt local resolution within 6 months; offer the patient the option of a meeting; provide a written response addressing all concerns; inform the patient of their right to take the complaint to the Parliamentary and Health Service Ombudsman (PHSO) if not satisfied. The complaint must be investigated and the patient kept informed of progress
options.C: Refer the complaint immediately to NHS England without any local resolution attempt
options.D: Ask the patient to complain in writing before acknowledging the complaint
options.E: Tell the patient that the GP's clinical judgment is not subject to complaint

explanation.correct: Per NHS Complaints Regulations 2009 (amended) and NHS England guidance, the practice must follow the NHS complaints procedure: (1) Acknowledge the complaint within 3 working days in writing; (2) Investigate the complaint promptly; (3) Aim to resolve within 6 months (complexity may extend this); (4) Offer a meeting with the patient if they wish; (5) Provide a written response addressing each concern; (6) Include an apology (without admission of liability) where appropriate; (7) Inform the patient of their right to refer to the Parliamentary and Health Service Ombudsman (PHSO) if not satisfied with the local resolution; (8) Keep a complaints register as part of clinical governance. The NHS complaint process does not prevent the patient from also seeking legal advice or reporting to the GMC/CQC.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Patients have a statutory right to complain under NHS Complaints Regulations 2009.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Acknowledge within 3 days, investigate, aim to resolve in 6 months, written response, inform of PHSO rights per NHS Complaints Regulations.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Local resolution must be attempted first — immediate escalation to NHS England without local process is not appropriate.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Complaints can be made verbally or in writing — the practice must acknowledge verbal complaints within the same timeframe.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Clinical judgment is not exempt from the complaints process — patients have the right to question clinical decisions through the complaints system.

reference: NHS Complaints Regulations 2009. NHS England — Complaints procedures. https://www.england.nhs.uk/ourwork/patient-participation/patient-and-public-participation/

question: A GP has been asked by a police officer who attends the practice to provide information about a patient who is suspected of a serious violent crime. The officer says the patient is dangerous and needs to be found. The GP has not received any formal court order or legal process. Per GMC confidentiality guidance, what should the GP do?

options.A: Provide all patient information immediately — police requests always override confidentiality
options.B: Police requests without a court order do not automatically override confidentiality. The GP should: consider whether there is a serious and credible risk of harm to others that outweighs the duty of confidentiality; can disclose the minimum necessary information in the public interest if the crime is serious (e.g., serious violence, murder) and disclosure could prevent serious harm; should ideally seek legal advice; document the decision-making process carefully. Disclosure without consent is only justified when: the benefit of disclosure outweighs the harm, the information cannot be obtained another way, disclosure is proportionate. Routine requests without this threshold do not require disclosure
options.C: Tell the police the patient is not registered at the practice — any response protects confidentiality
options.D: Provide name and address only — this is the minimum necessary for police purposes
options.E: Require a formal court order before any discussion — nothing else is acceptable

explanation.correct: Per GMC Confidentiality guidance (2017), disclosure to the police without consent may be justified in the public interest when: there is a risk of serious crime or serious harm to others; the benefit of disclosure outweighs confidentiality harm; the information is necessary and could not reasonably be obtained another way; disclosure is proportionate to the risk. GPs must not routinely disclose patient information to police on request — a police officer attending without a court order/production order (under PACE 1984 S9/Schedule 1) does not have an automatic right to medical records. The GP should: assess the specific risk; consider whether this is a genuine emergency; consult their medical defence organisation if time allows; document the decision carefully; disclose only the minimum necessary if public interest outweighs confidentiality.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Police requests without a court order do not automatically override confidentiality. Each request must be assessed on its merits.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Assess public interest threshold. Disclose minimum necessary only if serious harm risk outweighs confidentiality. Document carefully per GMC.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Providing false information to police is itself potentially a criminal offence. The GP should decline to confirm or deny without providing false information.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Even name and address requires the public interest threshold to be met — it cannot be provided as a routine response.
explanation.E: Incorrect — A court order is not always required — genuine public interest/serious harm situations can justify disclosure without a court order per GMC guidance.

reference: GMC — Confidentiality: good practice in handling patient information 2017. PACE 1984. https://www.gmc-uk.org/ethical-guidance/ethical-guidance-for-doctors/confidentiality

question: A 62-year-old man has been seeing his GP for several years. He presents with depression and during the consultation he discloses passive suicidal ideation. He has no active plans and says he would never act on it. He asks the GP not to tell anyone as he fears losing his job. Per GMC guidance and suicide prevention frameworks, what is the appropriate management?

options.A: Immediately hospitalise the patient and inform his employer
options.B: Conduct a thorough risk assessment (including thoughts, plans, intent, means, protective factors). Provide immediate therapeutic response — validate, explore the ideation, develop a safety plan. Consider urgent mental health team involvement if risk appears significant. Maintain confidentiality as requested if the risk does not constitute an immediate threat to life requiring disclosure. Document thoroughly. Arrange urgent follow-up. Provide crisis contact details (Samaritans, NHS 111, CRUSE)
options.C: Dismiss the passive ideation — patients who disclose suicidal thoughts never act on them
options.D: Inform his employer immediately — they need to know about the risk
options.E: Prescribe antidepressants and review in 6 weeks

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG222 (Self-harm: assessment, management and preventing recurrence, 2022) and Zero Suicide Alliance guidance, suicidal ideation requires a structured clinical response. The GP should: (1) Conduct a thorough risk assessment — not a checkbox exercise but a clinical conversation exploring nature of thoughts, any plans, intent, means, protective factors (social support, responsibilities, reasons for living); (2) Respond therapeutically — validate the patient's experience, maintain the therapeutic alliance; (3) Develop a collaborative safety plan; (4) Assess urgency — passive ideation without plan or intent = lower immediate risk but still significant; (5) Consider mental health team involvement; (6) Maintain confidentiality unless immediate threat to life; (7) Arrange urgent follow-up; (8) Provide crisis resources. Informing employer without consent would be a serious confidentiality breach — passive ideation without plan is not grounds for disclosure.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Passive ideation without active plan or intent does not automatically require hospital admission or employer notification.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Thorough risk assessment + safety plan + therapeutic response + confidentiality (unless immediate risk) + urgent follow-up per NICE NG222.
explanation.C: Incorrect — All suicidal ideation must be taken seriously — passive ideation is clinically significant and requires assessment.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Informing his employer without consent breaches confidentiality — passive suicidal ideation without imminent risk does not justify this disclosure.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Antidepressants take 4-6 weeks to work — prescribing and reviewing in 6 weeks without interim safety planning and follow-up for suicidal ideation is inadequate.

reference: NICE NG222 — Self-harm: assessment, management and preventing recurrence. Zero Suicide Alliance. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng222

question: A 30-year-old GP trainee (ST2) fails her MRCGP AKT examination for the second time and becomes very distressed. She confides in her educational supervisor that she feels completely unable to cope with the demands of general practice and wonders if she has made the wrong career choice. She has been attending work and has not made any clinical errors. Per GMC Good Medical Practice 2024 and the responsibility of educational supervisors, what should the educational supervisor do?

options.A: Immediately refer her to the GMC for fitness to practise concerns
options.B: Support the trainee compassionately: explore her distress and concerns; ensure she has access to occupational health and counselling (NHS Practitioner Health Programme); review her training needs and personal development plan; consider additional educational support for AKT; ensure she knows she can continue training while seeking support; only escalate to programme director if there are genuine patient safety concerns arising from her clinical performance. Emotional distress from exam failure is not a fitness to practise issue
options.C: Tell her to reconsider her career immediately — two AKT failures suggests she is not suitable for general practice
options.D: Add a negative supervisor's report to her e-portfolio noting she is not coping
options.E: No action — trainee wellbeing is not the educational supervisor's responsibility

explanation.correct: Per GMC Good Medical Practice 2024 and RCGP guidance on trainee support, the educational supervisor has a duty of care to their trainee. Emotional distress from exam failure is not a GMC fitness to practise matter unless it is affecting patient care. The supervisor should: (1) Create a safe, non-judgmental space for the trainee to express distress; (2) Signpost to occupational health and NHS Practitioner Health Programme (PHP); (3) Review the AKT preparation approach — consider additional resources, study leave, mock examinations; (4) Ensure the Personal Development Plan (PDP) addresses her learning needs; (5) Only escalate if there are genuine patient safety concerns from clinical practice; (6) Avoid adding negative entries to e-portfolio based on emotional distress rather than performance concerns. Trainee wellbeing is explicitly part of the educational supervisor's responsibilities per RCGP and GPST training programme requirements.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Exam failure and emotional distress is NOT a GMC fitness to practise concern unless patient safety is affected.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Support compassionately + occupational health/PHP + educational support + PDP review + only escalate if patient safety concerns. Per GMC and RCGP guidance.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Two AKT failures does not indicate unsuitability for general practice. Many successful GPs have required multiple attempts. Support and review is appropriate.
explanation.D: Incorrect — A negative e-portfolio entry based on emotional distress from exam failure rather than clinical performance would be inappropriate and potentially harmful.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Trainee wellbeing is explicitly part of the educational supervisor's role per RCGP and GMC guidance.

reference: GMC Good Medical Practice 2024. RCGP — Educational supervisor responsibilities. NHS Practitioner Health Programme. https://www.gmc-uk.org/ethical-guidance/ethical-guidance-for-doctors/good-medical-practice

question: A GP is asked to provide evidence for his annual appraisal. One of the domains requires evidence of quality improvement activity. Which of the following best describes what quality improvement evidence should include per the RCGP appraisal guidance?

options.A: A statement saying the GP 'aims to improve quality'
options.B: Evidence of participation in completed audit cycles, SEAs, QI projects or peer review — demonstrating reflection on findings, implementation of changes and re-measurement of outcomes. Evidence should show learning has occurred and changes have been implemented, not just that data was collected
options.C: Submission of patient satisfaction scores only
options.D: Evidence that no complaints have been received in the past year
options.E: A certificate from a management course

explanation.correct: Per RCGP appraisal guidance and GMC revalidation framework, quality improvement activity for appraisal must demonstrate: (1) Completed audit cycles (with re-measurement showing impact of changes); (2) Significant Event Analyses with documented learning and action plans; (3) Quality Improvement projects; (4) Peer review participation; (5) Clinical record reviews. Evidence requirements: demonstration that the GP has: identified a problem or learning opportunity; analysed it systematically; implemented change; re-evaluated outcomes. Crucially, incomplete audits (data collected but no change implemented or no re-audit) do not meet the quality improvement standard. The evidence must show reflection and genuine system improvement — not just data collection. GMC revalidation requires evidence from five domains including quality improvement at each 5-year cycle.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Aspirational statements without evidence of actual completed activities do not meet the appraisal standard.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Completed audit cycles with re-measurement + SEAs with action plans + QI projects demonstrating implementation and re-evaluation per RCGP guidance.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Patient satisfaction scores are relevant supporting evidence but are not the primary quality improvement evidence required.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Absence of complaints is not quality improvement evidence — it is a negative measure.
explanation.E: Incorrect — A management course certificate may be CPD evidence but is not quality improvement activity evidence.

reference: RCGP — Appraisal guidance. GMC — Revalidation: what you need to do. https://www.rcgp.org.uk/clinical-and-research/resources/quality-improvement-tools.aspx

question: A GP is running a minor surgery list. Between cases she is asked by a pharmaceutical company representative to review a drug's information leaflet as a 'consultancy service' for which she will receive payment. She has not declared this arrangement to the practice and there is no formal contract. Per GMC guidance on financial conflicts of interest and probity, what is the appropriate response?

options.A: Accept the payment — this is a legitimate additional income source for GPs
options.B: Decline to review during surgery time — any work for pharmaceutical companies must be: transparent; conducted outside clinical time; not influence clinical practice or prescribing; declared as a potential conflict of interest in relevant contexts (e.g., when advising on drug formularies, speaking to colleagues about the drug). All financial relationships with pharmaceutical organisations must be disclosed per GMC Good Medical Practice
options.C: Accept payment but do not mention it to anyone — financial arrangements are private
options.D: This is acceptable as long as the review is independent
options.E: Refer the representative to the practice manager for a commercial contract

explanation.correct: Per GMC Good Medical Practice 2024 (Domain 4 — Maintaining trust, paragraphs on probity and financial conflicts of interest): doctors must be honest and open about any financial interests that may influence their clinical practice or judgments. Working for pharmaceutical companies is not prohibited but must be: transparent (declared to employer/practice, in publications, when advising on prescribing); conducted separately from clinical practice time (during clinical time is inappropriate and potentially fraudulent use of NHS resources); not allowed to influence clinical decisions inappropriately; managed to avoid conflicts of interest. ABPI Code of Practice (Association of the British Pharmaceutical Industry) also governs interactions between pharma and clinicians. Undisclosed financial relationships with pharma companies that could influence prescribing behaviour are a probity concern.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Accepting payment during clinical surgery time uses NHS resources for private gain — this is an undisclosed conflict of interest.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Decline during clinical time. Pharma consultancy must be outside clinical time, transparent, declared as potential COI per GMC Good Medical Practice.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Financial arrangements with pharmaceutical companies must be disclosed, not kept private — GMC Good Medical Practice requires transparency.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Independence alone does not address the conflict of time (clinical vs private) and the need for transparency.
explanation.E: Incorrect — The practice manager referral does not address the immediate ethical issue of reviewing pharmaceutical materials during clinical surgery time.

reference: GMC Good Medical Practice 2024. ABPI Code of Practice. https://www.gmc-uk.org/ethical-guidance/ethical-guidance-for-doctors/good-medical-practice

question: A 72-year-old man with COPD and heart failure is admitted to hospital. He is not currently in a position to make decisions. His advance statement (not an ADRT — a statement of values and preferences) states he 'would prefer not to be admitted to hospital or receive aggressive treatment if possible.' He does not have LPA. His family wants 'everything done.' Per the MCA 2005, what weight does the advance statement carry?

options.A: The advance statement is legally binding — it must be followed exactly
options.B: An advance statement (statement of preferences and values — not an ADRT) is NOT legally binding but must be given serious weight in best interests decisions under MCA 2005. It is an important source of evidence about the patient's values and preferences that must be considered alongside: family views, clinical assessment, professional judgment. It does not override clinical decision-making but should significantly inform the best interests decision. The family's wishes are also a consultee input, not a decision
options.C: The family's decision to have 'everything done' overrides the advance statement
options.D: Without LPA, advance statements have no relevance to treatment decisions
options.E: The advance statement and family wishes cancel each other out — the clinical team decides independently

explanation.correct: Under the Mental Capacity Act 2005, there is a critical distinction: Advance Decision to Refuse Treatment (ADRT): legally binding if valid and applicable (must be in writing, signed, witnessed, specify the treatment being refused). Advance Statement (statement of preferences, values, wishes): NOT legally binding but must be given 'serious consideration' in best interests decisions under MCA 2005 Section 4(6)(a) — 'the person's past and present wishes and feelings...and the beliefs and values that would be likely to influence his decision.' The clinical team must: consider the advance statement as important evidence; consult family as consultees; make the best interests decision taking all evidence into account. The family's wishes are consultee input — they inform but do not determine the decision. The advance statement expressing preference against aggressive hospital treatment is clinically significant — it represents the patient's values when capacitous.
explanation.A: Incorrect — An advance STATEMENT (of preferences/values) is NOT legally binding — only an ADRT is legally binding when valid and applicable.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Advance statement must be given serious weight in MCA 2005 best interests decision. Family are consultees not decision-makers. Clinicians make the decision.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Family wishes are consultee input — they do not override the patient's expressed preferences in an advance statement.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Advance statements are relevant and must be considered under MCA 2005 Section 4(6) — LPA is not required for their consideration.
explanation.E: Incorrect — The clinical team does not decide independently — they must give serious weight to the advance statement and family input in the structured best interests framework.

reference: Mental Capacity Act 2005 — Section 4. MCA Code of Practice. https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2005/9/contents

question: A GP practice manager informs the GP partners that the practice's network (PCN) has been asked to implement a new diabetes care pathway that includes a Patient Participation Group (PPG) review. A partner asks what the PPG is and what role they play per NHS England guidance.

options.A: PPG is an optional committee with no formal role in practice governance
options.B: Patient Participation Groups (PPGs) are a required component of GP practices under NHS England directions. PPGs: represent patient and community perspectives in practice decisions; are consulted on proposed changes to services; review and provide feedback on practice performance; help develop patient information materials; contribute to the practice's patient experience improvement plans. Per NHS England guidance (as a condition of the GP contract), practices must establish and maintain a PPG and take account of its views
options.C: PPGs have the right to veto any clinical decision made by the GP partners
options.D: PPGs are only required in practices with more than 5000 registered patients
options.E: PPGs are voluntary bodies with no contractual requirement

explanation.correct: Patient Participation Groups (PPGs) are required under the GMS/PMS contract directed by NHS England. Per the NHS Patients' right to be involved, GPs must: establish and maintain a PPG; seek their views; use their feedback to develop an annual practice development plan; publish a patient participation report annually. PPG roles: patient perspective input into service development; patient experience surveys; review of patient-facing communications; development of health promotion activities; input into access and appointment policies. PPGs are consultative — they provide input to decision-making but do not have veto power over clinical or operational decisions. They are part of the broader NHS England commitment to patient and public participation in healthcare.
explanation.A: Incorrect — PPGs are a contractual requirement, not optional.
explanation.B: CORRECT — PPGs are required under GP contract. Represent patient perspectives. Consulted on service changes. Practice must act on their views per NHS England.
explanation.C: Incorrect — PPGs are consultative — they do not have veto power over clinical decisions.
explanation.D: Incorrect — The PPG requirement applies to all GP practices regardless of list size.
explanation.E: Incorrect — PPGs are a contractual requirement under the GMS/PMS contract — not voluntary.

reference: NHS England — Patient participation directions. GMS Contract. https://www.england.nhs.uk/gp/investment/gp-contract/

question: A 45-year-old teacher is seeking a sick note (fit note) from her GP. She has been off work with moderate depression for 3 weeks and is feeling somewhat better. She asks if she can return to work on a phased return. Per the current fit note system (Statement of Fitness for Work) introduced in 2010, what can the GP document?

options.A: Fit notes can only state 'fit for work' or 'not fit for work' — no intermediate options
options.B: The current Statement of Fitness for Work (fit note) has four options: (1) 'May be fit for work' — with specified adjustments (amended duties, altered hours, workplace adaptations, phased return to work); (2) 'Not fit for work'; (3) If the GP ticks 'may be fit for work' with phased return: the employer and employee discuss whether adjustments are possible; if not, the patient is treated as unfit. GPs are not required to complete fit notes for the first 7 days of absence
options.C: Only hospital specialists can sign fit notes for mental health conditions
options.D: Fit notes must be signed by a GP — nurses and physiotherapists cannot sign them
options.E: Fit notes are only valid for conditions lasting longer than 4 weeks

explanation.correct: The Statement of Fitness for Work (fit note) was introduced in April 2010, replacing the old 'sick note'. Key features: (1) Options: 'Not fit for work' (specific period) OR 'May be fit for work' with functional effects described and one or more recommended adjustments (phased return to work, amended duties, altered hours, workplace adaptations); (2) If 'may be fit for work' is selected: employer and employee discuss; if adjustments not possible, the note is treated as 'not fit for work'; (3) No fit note required for first 7 days of absence — self-certification is used; (4) Fit notes can be signed by doctors, nurse practitioners, physiotherapists, occupational therapists and pharmacists (extended to allied health professionals in 2022); (5) Fit notes can cover periods retrospectively. For moderate depression showing improvement, 'may be fit for work' with phased return is clinically appropriate and supports recovery.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Fit notes introduced in 2010 specifically added 'may be fit for work' as a third option, with the ability to recommend adjustments.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Fit note options: 'not fit for work' or 'may be fit for work' with adjustments (phased return, amended duties, altered hours). No fit note needed for first 7 days.
explanation.C: Incorrect — GPs can sign fit notes for mental health conditions — specialist referral is not required for fit note completion.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Since 2022, fit notes can be signed by nurses, physiotherapists, occupational therapists and pharmacists in addition to doctors.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Fit notes are not limited to conditions lasting longer than 4 weeks — they apply from day 8 of absence onwards.

reference: DWP — Statement of Fitness for Work guidance. Fit note reform 2010/2022. https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/fit-note

question: A 40-year-old woman with a known personality disorder diagnosis has a long and complex medical history. During a consultation about a new physical symptom (back pain), the GP notices she feels dismissed and undervalued. She says 'you just think I'm attention-seeking because of my mental health.' The GP has limited time. Per the Equality Act 2010, the NHS Constitution and good practice in managing patients with complex needs, what are the key obligations?

options.A: Document 'frequent attender' in the notes and limit consultation time
options.B: Provide equitable, non-discriminatory care: the Equality Act 2010 protects individuals from discrimination based on disability (mental health conditions qualify). A personality disorder diagnosis must not bias the assessment of physical symptoms. The GP must: validate the patient's experience; take the back pain seriously; conduct a thorough assessment; document clearly and without stigmatising language. Consider the NHS Constitution: patients have the right to be treated with dignity and respect. Coordinate care with the community mental health team. Adjust consultation length if needed (reasonable adjustment)
options.C: Refer to mental health services — the back pain is likely psychosomatic
options.D: Limit consultations to 10 minutes per NHS GP contract — legal obligation
options.E: Patients with personality disorder diagnoses cannot expect the same level of clinical assessment as other patients

explanation.correct: Per the Equality Act 2010, mental health conditions that substantially affect day-to-day activities (including personality disorder) constitute a disability under the Act. The NHS has a duty not to discriminate in provision of services and to make reasonable adjustments. Key obligations: (1) Non-discrimination — a personality disorder diagnosis must not bias assessment of physical symptoms (diagnostic overshadowing — attributing physical symptoms to mental health diagnosis — is a recognised and harmful clinical bias); (2) NHS Constitution rights — be treated with dignity and respect; access to healthcare; (3) Reasonable adjustments — longer appointments, case coordination, care plans; (4) Documentation — use dignified, non-stigmatising language in notes; (5) Collaboration — work with mental health services. The stigma associated with personality disorder diagnoses significantly contributes to health inequalities and premature mortality in this population.
explanation.A: Incorrect — 'Frequent attender' labelling and limiting time without clinical justification is discriminatory and risks missing serious pathology.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Equitable, non-discriminatory care. Equality Act 2010 protection. Reasonable adjustment (longer appointment). Diagnostic overshadowing must be avoided per NHS Constitution.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Dismissing physical symptoms as psychosomatic based on mental health diagnosis is diagnostic overshadowing — a form of bias that must be avoided.
explanation.D: Incorrect — There is no fixed 10-minute legal obligation per GP contract — appointment length is a clinical decision. Reasonable adjustments may require longer appointments.
explanation.E: Incorrect — All patients have equal rights to clinical assessment under the Equality Act 2010 and NHS Constitution — diagnosis must not reduce entitlement to care.

reference: Equality Act 2010. NHS Constitution. GMC Good Medical Practice 2024. https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2010/15/contents

question: A GP is treating a patient who has recently been released from prison. The patient is requesting their records from before their imprisonment. They mention that during their time in prison they developed hepatitis C and received treatment. Per UK GDPR and NHS guidance, does a patient's previous incarceration affect their right to access their medical records?

options.A: Prisoners lose the right to access medical records upon conviction
options.B: No — a person's history of incarceration does not affect their UK GDPR Article 15 right to access their personal data. The GP practice must respond to a valid subject access request within one month, free of charge, regardless of the patient's past. Records from the prison healthcare period (held by the prison healthcare service, not the GP) would require a separate SAR to the relevant prison trust. All patients have equal data rights under UK GDPR
options.C: Only recent (post-release) records can be accessed
options.D: Former prisoners must provide proof of identity before accessing records — unlike other patients
options.E: Records from before imprisonment are automatically deleted by NHS systems after 2 years

explanation.correct: UK GDPR (UK General Data Protection Regulation) establishes data rights that apply to all individuals in the UK regardless of criminal history, immigration status, or other personal circumstances. The right of access (Article 15) allows any data subject to request and receive copies of their personal data held by a controller. The GP practice must: respond within one month; provide the requested records free of charge; apply only the standard limited exceptions (harm to self/third party, third-party data). A person's conviction history does not create any additional barriers to their data rights. Records held during imprisonment are held by NHS England/prison healthcare trust — a separate SAR to that organisation would be required. The ICO confirms that criminal convictions do not affect an individual's data rights under UK GDPR.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Criminal conviction does not affect UK GDPR rights. Data subject rights apply equally to all individuals.
explanation.B: CORRECT — All individuals including former prisoners have equal UK GDPR Article 15 rights. Prison healthcare records are held by a separate trust and require a separate SAR.
explanation.C: Incorrect — The right of access applies to all personal data held — not limited to recent records.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Proof of identity verification requirements are the same for all patients — not enhanced for former prisoners.
explanation.E: Incorrect — NHS medical records are retained according to NHS Records Management Code of Practice — not automatically deleted after 2 years.

reference: UK GDPR Article 15. ICO — Right of access. NHS Records Management Code of Practice. https://ico.org.uk/for-organisations/uk-gdpr-guidance-and-resources/individual-rights/

question: A 28-year-old woman discloses to her GP that she is a sex worker. She asks for confidential sexual health testing. She expresses fear that her profession will be shared with other healthcare providers. Per GMC confidentiality guidance and UK GDPR, what assurances can the GP give regarding confidentiality?

options.A: Sex work is a criminal activity — the GP must report this to the police
options.B: The GP can assure her that: her disclosure will be treated in strict confidence per GMC confidentiality guidance and UK GDPR; information will only be shared with other healthcare providers who have a direct need to know for her care (on a 'need to know' basis and in her best interests); it will not be shared with police, immigration services or other agencies unless there is an immediate risk to life; she has the right to request that sensitive information be restricted in the electronic record. Providing non-judgmental, accessible healthcare to marginalised populations is a core professional duty
options.C: Sex work must be recorded on the medical record and automatically shared with all healthcare providers
options.D: The GP cannot provide confidential sexual health testing — this must be done at a GUM clinic
options.E: The GP must immediately refer to social services as sex work indicates vulnerability

explanation.correct: Per GMC confidentiality guidance and UK GDPR: (1) Sex work in England and Wales is not itself illegal (though associated activities may be) — it is not a reportable matter; (2) Information shared in a clinical consultation is held in strict confidence; (3) Sharing with other healthcare providers: on a 'need to know' basis for direct care only — unnecessary disclosure of occupational information is a breach of confidentiality; (4) The patient can request sensitive information be restricted in shared records (Summary Care Record — patients can request restriction of specific information); (5) The GP should provide non-judgmental, equitable healthcare. Equity in healthcare access is a professional duty — marginalised populations including sex workers have equal rights to confidential healthcare. The doctor's role is to provide healthcare, not to judge occupational choices. Disclosure to police or immigration services would not be justified in these circumstances.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Sex work (selling sex) is not illegal in England and Wales — it is not reportable to police.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Strict confidentiality applies. Need-to-know sharing only. Patient can request restriction. Non-judgmental care is a professional duty per GMC.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Occupational information must be shared only on a need-to-know basis — automatic sharing with all providers would breach UK GDPR and GMC confidentiality guidance.
explanation.D: Incorrect — GP practices can provide sexual health testing. GUM clinics are not the only option — reducing barriers to healthcare access is important for this population.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Sex work alone does not automatically trigger social services referral. There may be safeguarding concerns in specific circumstances, but employment as a sex worker is not itself a mandatory referral trigger.

reference: GMC — Confidentiality: good practice in handling patient information. UK GDPR. https://www.gmc-uk.org/ethical-guidance/ethical-guidance-for-doctors/confidentiality
